title.narrative: 2026 - Remote data and digital support for Venezuela

description.narrative: Concretely, it means two channels working together: Red Cross volunteers going door to door with a simple digital form, and a WhatsApp line people can message directly. Both feed into one shared database, so nothing falls through the cracks, and there's someone whose job it is to read the feedback, act on it, and let the person know what happened as a result. That last part matters a lot: past earthquake responses elsewhere showed that when people give feedback and never hear back, they stop trusting the aid effort. This project is built specifically to avoid that.

The Venezuela earthquake response is a Red-level, CHF 50 million IFRC Emergency Appeal (MDRVE015) targeting 300,000 people, with over 5,500 confirmed fatalities, 46 transitional camps, and up to 38 damaged hospitals. NLRC/510's rationale for intervening remotely rests on a specific evidence-based risk: past large responses (Türkiye/Syria, Ukraine, Nepal Karnali) show that community feedback systems get built technically but fail because National Society digital literacy and absorption capacity aren't matched, closing-the-loop practice isn't documented, and institutional ownership doesn't outlast the surge. The proposal exists to prevent that pattern from repeating here, at a scale proportionate to the appeal.

The direct beneficiaries are the up to 300,000 people targeted by the Emergency Appeal, particularly those in transitional camps and spontaneous settlements who need a functioning, trusted feedback channel. The capacity-building beneficiary is the Venezuelan Red Cross (Cruz Roja Venezolana), which owns the response and will run CFM/WhatsApp operationally after NLRC/510 hands it over, specifically its CEA focal point (Solis) and the operators and volunteers trained under the ToT model. IFRC is the coordinating body under the Appeal, and NLRC/510 positions itself explicitly as a remote technical enabler, not the consortium lead.

The response covers Venezuela's most-affected states, La Guaira, Caracas (Capital District), Miranda, Falcón, Carabobo, and Yaracuy, plus areas receiving displaced populations. Connectivity is a real constraint in some of these zones; La Guaira in particular is reported to have very limited internet, with Starlink and portable antennas already deployed there for registration activities and flagged as reusable for CFM training.

This is a proposal for the Netherlands Red Cross's data team (510) to remotely help the Venezuelan Red Cross set up a proper way to listen to people affected by the earthquake and respond to them. Right now, when someone affected by the disaster wants to ask a question, report a problem, or give feedback about the aid they're receiving, there's no single, reliable system to catch that and make sure someone follows up. This project builds that system.
